source_text: Verum ut ambos vos veritas detexit, et proruit; ita a nobis consideratio nostri reposcit officii, ut quid sit hoc quod obscuritatem huic quaestioni, quae iam exarmata est, fecerat, explicemus. Omnia quae fiunt, aut a necessario, aut a possibili dicuntur existere. Necessarium autem hic dico, non quod solemus utile nuncupare, sed quod maioribus fuerit causis coactum. Necessarium ergo vocamus, non quod in iure sit voluntatis, sed quod patiatur existendi vim. Possibile autem dicimus, quod nec existendi, nec non existendi in alteram partem experiatur necessitatem, sed certis modis et possit esse, et possit non esse. Teneat ergo lector noster, quid hic necessarium, quid possibile nuncupemus. Et ut a grandibus inchoemus exemplis, ut Deus faceret mundum, a possibili venit, non a necessario; id est, omnipotentiae eius possibile fuit creare quae condidit, necessarium tamen non fuit, videlicet non est ab aliquo coactus ut faceret, sed fecit quia voluit, quod non fecisset profecto si noluisset. At hoc quod auctori adfuit a possibili, in opere a necessario factum est, id est, non fuit mundo possibile esse et non esse, qui esse ab Omnipotente iubebatur, sed cogebatur existere, cui Omnipotens mandabat essentiam.
pass_a_gloss: But as truth detected both of you, and overthrew; so consideration of our office demands from us that we explain what this is which had made obscurity for this question, which has already been disarmed. All things which are made are said to exist either from the necessary or from the possible. But I say necessary here, not what we are accustomed to name useful, but what has been compelled by greater causes. We therefore call necessary not what is in the right of will, but what suffers a force of existing. But we say possible what experiences a necessity of existing or of not existing toward neither part, but by certain measures both can be and can not be. Let our reader therefore hold what we name here necessary, what possible. And that we may begin from great examples, that God made the world came from the possible, not from the necessary; that is, it was possible for his omnipotence to create what he founded, yet it was not necessary, namely he was not compelled by anyone that he make, but he made because he willed, which he would certainly not have made if he had been unwilling. But this which was present to the author from the possible was made in the work from the necessary, that is, it was not possible for the world to be and not to be, which was being commanded to be by the Omnipotent, but it was compelled to exist, to whom the Omnipotent was mandating essence.

pass_b_english: But just as truth has exposed and overthrown you both, so consideration of our duty requires us to explain what made this now-disarmed question obscure. Everything that occurs is said to arise either from necessity or from possibility. By ‘necessary’ here I mean not what we ordinarily call useful, but what is compelled by stronger causes. We therefore call necessary not what lies within the will’s authority, but what is subject to a force requiring its existence. We call possible what undergoes no necessity on either side, either to exist or not to exist, but in definite ways can exist and can fail to exist. Let our reader hold firmly to what we mean here by necessary and possible.

To begin with great examples: God’s making the world arose from possibility, not necessity. That is, his almighty power made it possible to create what he formed, but not necessary. No one compelled him to make it; he made it because he willed to, and certainly would not have made it had he not willed to. Yet what belonged to the maker as a possibility became a necessity in the work. The world, commanded to exist by the Almighty, did not have the possibility both of existing and not existing: it was compelled to exist, since the Almighty commanded its being.
